questions.question: Why is client-side validation insufficient as a security control?
questions.option_a: A browser user can modify or bypass client-side checks before sending a request.
questions.option_b: Client-side validation encrypts data too early.
questions.option_c: The server cannot receive form data after validation.
questions.explanation: The client is controlled by the user. The server must validate and authorise every request independently.

questions.question: Which sequence best represents a typical web interaction?
questions.option_a: A response is sent before the browser makes a request.
questions.option_b: The browser sends an HTTP request and the server returns an HTTP response.
questions.option_c: The database sends an HTTP request directly to the browser.
questions.option_d: The browser executes the server database query locally.
questions.explanation: The browser/client initiates an HTTP request; the server processes it and returns a response.

questions.question: A tester changes a hidden form field from role=user to role=admin. What is the key security question?
questions.option_a: Whether the field is visually hidden.
questions.option_b: Whether the browser accepts the modified value.
questions.option_c: Whether the server independently verifies the requested privilege.
questions.option_d: Whether the field is encoded in Base64.
questions.explanation: Hidden fields are client-controlled state. The server must not trust them to establish permissions.

questions.question: Which HTTP status most directly indicates that the server understood the request but refused access?
questions.option_a: 200 OK
questions.explanation: 403 indicates the server understood the request but refuses to authorise it.

questions.question: A protected endpoint redirects an unauthenticated user to the login page. Which status might commonly accompany this behaviour?
questions.option_a: 302 Found
questions.explanation: A 302 redirect can send the browser to a login page; the status alone does not prove access control is correctly implemented.

questions.question: Which statement about a bearer token is correct?
questions.option_a: It is safe to expose because it contains no password.
questions.option_b: Possession of the token can be sufficient to exercise the associated authority.
questions.option_c: It is valid only when stored in localStorage.
questions.option_d: It cannot be replayed by another client.
questions.explanation: Bearer credentials are usable by whoever possesses them, so they must be protected against disclosure and replay.

questions.question: A tester can alter a request body but the page UI prevents selecting another account ID. What is the most reliable test approach?
questions.option_a: Trust the UI and stop testing that field.
questions.option_b: Inspect and modify the raw HTTP request, then observe the server response.
questions.option_c: Disable JavaScript and assume the endpoint is secure.
questions.explanation: The server consumes the HTTP request, not the UI’s intended controls. Raw request tampering tests the actual trust boundary.

questions.question: An endpoint returns 200 for a modified request, but the response contains the same user data as before. What can be concluded?
questions.option_a: A vulnerability is proven because the status is 200.
questions.option_c: The status alone is insufficient; compare response content and application behaviour to establish impact.
questions.option_d: The server must be using JWT.
questions.explanation: A successful HTTP status does not prove unauthorised access. The actual returned data or action must be examined.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of application mapping during a web penetration test?
questions.option_a: To identify pages, endpoints, parameters, technologies and application behaviour.
questions.option_b: To immediately exploit every discovered endpoint.
questions.explanation: Mapping builds an understanding of the application attack surface before targeted testing.

questions.question: Which source is most useful for discovering links and routes embedded in client-side JavaScript?
questions.option_a: A password hash list.
questions.option_b: JavaScript files and their referenced endpoints.
questions.option_c: The operating system event log only.
questions.option_d: A database backup unrelated to the application.
questions.explanation: Client-side scripts can reveal API routes, hidden functionality and parameter names.

questions.question: What is the main difference between passive mapping and active content discovery?
questions.option_a: Passive mapping never observes application responses.
questions.option_b: Active discovery sends requests to candidate paths; passive mapping observes available traffic and content.
questions.option_d: Active discovery is always invisible to the server.
questions.explanation: Active tools probe candidate paths, while passive techniques infer structure from observed application content and traffic.

questions.question: A tester wants to discover hidden directories using a wordlist. Which tool category is appropriate?
questions.option_a: Directory/content discovery tools such as ffuf or gobuster.
questions.explanation: ffuf and gobuster can request candidate paths from a wordlist and identify interesting responses.

questions.question: Why should an application be mapped both while logged out and while authenticated?
questions.option_a: Authentication changes the HTTP protocol.
questions.option_b: Authenticated users may expose additional pages, endpoints and functions unavailable to anonymous visitors.
questions.option_d: The two maps must always be identical.
questions.explanation: Different roles and session states can expose different parts of the attack surface.

questions.question: A content-discovery scan reports many paths with identical response lengths and status codes. What is the best next step?
questions.option_a: Treat every result as a confirmed vulnerability.
questions.option_b: Tune filtering or baseline comparisons to distinguish default/error responses from meaningful content.
questions.option_d: Assume the server has no endpoints.
questions.explanation: Response status and length need contextual interpretation; generic fallback pages can create false positives.

questions.question: Which statement best describes the relationship between OWASP WSTG and OWASP Top 10?
questions.option_a: They are interchangeable lists of the same ten vulnerabilities.
questions.option_b: The Top 10 is an awareness-level risk overview; WSTG provides more detailed testing guidance.
questions.option_d: The Top 10 replaces the need for methodology.
questions.explanation: The lecture positions the Top 10 as a shared risk vocabulary and WSTG as a more exhaustive testing methodology.

questions.question: A tester finds /admin in a wordlist scan. Which conclusion is justified before testing access?
questions.option_a: The application has Broken Access Control.
questions.option_c: A potentially sensitive endpoint exists; its access restrictions and actions must be tested.
questions.option_d: The endpoint must be removed from the report.
questions.explanation: Discovery alone does not establish a vulnerability. The tester must check whether unauthorised users can access the page or its functions.

questions.question: What is Burp Suite Proxy primarily used for?
questions.option_a: Intercepting, inspecting and modifying HTTP requests and responses.
questions.explanation: Burp Proxy sits between browser and server so traffic can be inspected and modified.

questions.question: What is the default Burp listener address and port shown in the lecture setup?
questions.explanation: The lecture configures the Burp listener at 127.0.0.1:8080.

questions.question: Why is Burp’s CA certificate installed in the browser for HTTPS interception?
questions.option_a: To let Burp decrypt database backups.
questions.option_b: To make the browser trust Burp’s certificate when Burp intercepts TLS connections.
questions.option_c: To disable HTTPS on the target server.
questions.option_d: To authenticate the tester as an administrator.
questions.explanation: The browser must trust Burp’s CA to avoid certificate errors when Burp generates certificates for intercepted HTTPS sites.

questions.question: Which Burp tool is best suited to manually edit and resend one captured request repeatedly?
questions.option_a: Comparer
questions.explanation: Repeater is designed for manual request modification and resending.

questions.question: Which Burp tool automates sending many requests while changing marked payload positions?
questions.option_a: Intruder
questions.explanation: Intruder inserts payloads at marked positions and sends repeated requests.

questions.question: Which Intruder attack type uses one payload set and inserts the same payload into all marked positions?
questions.option_a: Sniper
questions.explanation: Battering ram applies the same payload value to every marked position for each request.

questions.question: Two Intruder payload positions each have their own list, and the tester wants corresponding first, second, third entries paired together. Which mode fits?
questions.option_a: Cluster bomb
questions.explanation: Pitchfork iterates through multiple payload sets in parallel, pairing corresponding positions.

questions.question: A tester has 20 usernames and 50 passwords and wants every possible username-password combination. Which Intruder mode and request count are expected?
questions.option_a: Pitchfork; 70 requests
questions.explanation: Cluster bomb tests all combinations; 20 × 50 = 1,000 requests.

questions.question: What is the purpose of Burp Comparer?
questions.option_a: To compare two responses and identify differences.
questions.option_d: To generate a TLS certificate for the server.
questions.explanation: Comparer provides word- or byte-level differences between selected messages.

questions.question: In the lecture’s login workflow, why is a successful response compared with a failed response?
questions.option_a: To prove that the password is encrypted.
questions.option_b: To identify response differences that distinguish successful authentication from failure.
questions.option_d: To determine the server’s physical location.
questions.explanation: Comparing responses can reveal a reliable success indicator such as a different length or content.

questions.question: Which OWASP Top 10 edition is the examination baseline stated in the lecture?
questions.explanation: The lecture explicitly says the course is examined on the OWASP Top 10:2021 list.

questions.question: Which category is A01 in OWASP Top 10:2021?
questions.option_a: Cryptographic Failures
questions.explanation: A01:2021 is Broken Access Control.

questions.question: Which category is A10 in OWASP Top 10:2021?
questions.option_a: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF)
questions.explanation: A10:2021 is Server-Side Request Forgery.

questions.question: Which statement about the OWASP Top 10 is most accurate according to the lecture?
questions.option_a: It is a complete testing checklist.
questions.option_b: It is an awareness document and shared risk vocabulary, not an exhaustive checklist.
questions.explanation: The lecture distinguishes the Top 10 awareness overview from exhaustive testing guidance such as WSTG.

questions.question: Authentication answers which question?
questions.option_a: What are you allowed to do?
questions.explanation: Authentication establishes identity; authorisation determines permitted actions and resources.

questions.question: Authorisation should be checked at what point?
questions.option_a: Only when the user logs in.
questions.option_b: Only when the page is rendered.
questions.option_c: On every request for the requested resource or function.
questions.explanation: The lecture stresses checking authorisation for each request and resource.

questions.question: A normal user accesses an administrator-only function. What type of access-control failure is this?
questions.option_a: Horizontal privilege escalation
questions.explanation: Vertical access-control failure occurs when a user reaches a higher privilege level.

questions.question: A user accesses another user’s invoice while remaining at the same privilege level. What is this?
questions.option_a: Vertical access-control failure
questions.explanation: Horizontal access control concerns access to another user’s resources at the same privilege level.

questions.question: What does IDOR stand for?
questions.option_a: Insecure Direct Object Reference
questions.explanation: IDOR means Insecure Direct Object Reference.

questions.question: A request uses GET /api/orders?id=1042. Changing the ID returns another customer’s order while keeping the original user token. What is the likely flaw?
questions.option_a: IDOR caused by missing ownership authorisation.
questions.explanation: The server accepted a client-controlled object reference without verifying that the authenticated user owns the order.

questions.question: Which test setup is recommended for systematically testing IDOR in the lecture?
questions.option_a: One administrator account only.
questions.option_b: Two accounts, A and B, with known object references for each.
questions.option_d: A production customer account without permission.
questions.explanation: Two accounts let the tester attempt cross-account access and compare it with legitimate access.

questions.question: Why is a same-account positive control important during IDOR testing?
questions.option_a: It increases the number of requests.
questions.option_b: It confirms the request works for the rightful owner, so a failed cross-account attempt is meaningful.
questions.option_d: It proves the identifier is unpredictable.
questions.explanation: The positive control distinguishes an authorisation denial from a malformed or otherwise broken request.

questions.question: A normal user receives 403 for /admin, but POST /api/user/delete succeeds for the same user. What does this suggest?
questions.option_a: The page is protected but the underlying action endpoint may lack function-level access control.
questions.option_b: The user has no valid session.
questions.option_c: The endpoint is protected because /admin returned 403.
questions.option_d: The issue is only a browser rendering bug.
questions.explanation: The lecture warns that testers must examine actions and API endpoints, not only the hidden page.

questions.question: Why is relying on a hidden navigation link not sufficient to protect an administrative function?
questions.option_a: URLs cannot be guessed.
questions.option_b: An attacker may discover or directly request the endpoint without using the UI.
questions.option_d: Browsers enforce role permissions on links.
questions.explanation: Security by obscurity fails when a user directly requests a known or discovered URL.

questions.question: Which server-side rule most directly prevents IDOR?
questions.option_a: Use longer sequential numeric IDs.
questions.option_b: Verify that the authenticated principal is authorised to access the specific object on every request.
questions.explanation: Unpredictable IDs are not a substitute for checking ownership and permissions.

questions.question: A tester changes an invoice ID; the server returns 404 for another user’s invoice but 200 for their own. What is the strongest interpretation?
questions.option_a: The application is definitely vulnerable because 404 reveals existence.
questions.option_b: The observed behaviour is consistent with an ownership check or concealed denial; further authorised tests are needed before claiming a bypass.
questions.option_d: The tester has proven vertical escalation.
questions.explanation: A 404 can be used to conceal resource existence. The evidence shown does not establish unauthorised access.

questions.question: Which option best describes credential stuffing?
questions.option_a: Trying one common password against many accounts.
questions.option_b: Reusing username-password pairs leaked from other services to attempt logins.
questions.option_c: Guessing every possible password for one account.
questions.option_d: Changing an account ID in an API request.
questions.explanation: Credential stuffing uses previously exposed credential pairs, often at scale.

questions.question: How does password spraying differ from brute-forcing one account?
questions.option_a: Password spraying tries a small set of common passwords across many accounts.
questions.option_b: Password spraying changes the URL path only.
questions.explanation: Password spraying distributes guesses across accounts to reduce the chance of triggering per-account lockouts.

questions.question: An application reveals “username does not exist” for one input and “wrong password” for another. What weakness may this create?
questions.option_a: Username enumeration
questions.explanation: Different responses can reveal which usernames are registered.

questions.question: Which cookie attribute prevents JavaScript from reading a cookie through document.cookie?
questions.option_a: Secure
questions.explanation: HttpOnly restricts access to the cookie from client-side scripts.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the Secure cookie attribute?
questions.option_a: Send the cookie only over secure HTTPS connections.
questions.option_b: Prevent the server from reading the cookie.
questions.option_c: Encrypt the cookie payload using JWT.
questions.option_d: Make the cookie available to every domain.
questions.explanation: Secure instructs the browser to send the cookie over secure connections.

questions.question: What does SameSite primarily help mitigate?
questions.option_a: Cross-site request contexts, including some CSRF scenarios.
questions.explanation: SameSite controls when cookies are sent in cross-site contexts and can reduce CSRF exposure.

questions.question: Which statement about JWT payloads is correct?
questions.option_a: They are always encrypted.
questions.option_b: They are commonly Base64url-encoded and can be decoded; encoding is not encryption.
questions.option_d: They are stored only in HTTP headers by definition.
questions.explanation: A typical signed JWT payload is readable after Base64url decoding; the signature protects integrity, not confidentiality.

questions.question: A JWT verifier accepts a token after the algorithm is changed to none and the signature is removed. What is the likely issue?
questions.option_a: Improper JWT algorithm/signature validation.
questions.explanation: The verifier must enforce an allowed signing algorithm and require valid signature verification.

questions.question: Why should session identifiers be invalidated after logout or a security-sensitive account change?
questions.option_a: To reduce the chance that a previously issued session remains usable.
questions.explanation: Session invalidation prevents continued use of credentials that should no longer be trusted.

questions.question: A login endpoint returns identical messages for valid and invalid usernames, but response times consistently differ. What should the tester consider?
questions.option_a: Timing-based username enumeration may still be possible.
questions.explanation: Even when messages match, measurable timing differences can reveal account existence or processing paths.

questions.question: Which principle best addresses both client-controlled role fields and client-controlled object IDs?
questions.option_a: Trust the browser after login.
questions.option_b: Treat client input as untrusted and enforce identity, ownership and permissions server-side.
questions.explanation: Both issues arise when the server trusts client-controlled values instead of enforcing server-side security decisions.

questions.question: A tester finds a valid session token can read another user’s record. Which control is missing even though authentication works?
questions.option_a: TLS encryption
questions.explanation: A valid session proves identity, not permission to access every object.

questions.question: What is the root cause of SQL injection?
questions.option_a: User input is concatenated into SQL in a way that changes the query’s intended structure.
questions.explanation: SQLi occurs when untrusted input is interpreted as part of SQL syntax rather than as data.

questions.question: Which input is a common first probe for detecting string-context SQL injection?
questions.option_a: A single quote (')
questions.explanation: A single quote can expose syntax errors or alter a quoted SQL expression.

questions.question: In a login form, why can an input such as admin'-- - alter a vulnerable SQL query?
questions.option_a: It changes the page CSS.
questions.option_b: It may close a quoted string and comment out the remainder of the SQL statement.
questions.option_d: It creates a new database user automatically.
questions.explanation: The quote can terminate a string literal and the SQL comment can neutralise the remaining predicate, depending on query syntax and database behaviour.

questions.question: What is the purpose of testing a Boolean condition that should be true and one that should be false?
questions.option_a: To identify a Boolean-based SQL injection by observing different application behaviour.
questions.explanation: A vulnerable application may behave differently when the injected SQL predicate evaluates true versus false.

questions.question: What does UNION-based SQL injection attempt to do?
questions.option_a: Combine results from an attacker-controlled SELECT with the original query’s result set.
questions.explanation: UNION can make the database return data from another SELECT when column counts and compatible types align.

questions.question: Why might a tester use ORDER BY with increasing column indexes during UNION testing?
questions.option_a: To discover how many columns the original query returns.
questions.option_b: To determine the server’s MAC address.
questions.explanation: An out-of-range ORDER BY column can trigger an error, helping infer the result-set column count.

questions.question: A UNION payload fails because the injected SELECT has a different number of columns from the original query. What must be done?
questions.option_a: Match the original result column count, using suitable placeholder values where needed.
questions.option_b: Change the HTTP method to TRACE.
questions.explanation: UNION queries generally need compatible column counts and data types across the SELECT statements.

questions.question: The application displays no database errors or query results, but its response changes when a predicate is true versus false. Which technique is indicated?
questions.option_a: Boolean-based blind SQL injection
questions.explanation: Boolean-based blind SQLi infers information from observable differences in application responses.

questions.question: A tester observes a deliberate delay only when an injected SQL condition is true. What technique is being used?
questions.option_a: Time-based blind SQL injection
questions.explanation: Time-based blind SQLi uses conditional database delays as an inference channel.

questions.question: What is a stacked-query injection?
questions.option_a: Submitting multiple SQL statements where the database driver and context permit them.
questions.explanation: Stacked queries attempt to execute an additional SQL statement after the original one; support depends on the database and driver.

questions.question: What is second-order SQL injection?
questions.option_a: Input is stored first and later used unsafely in a SQL query, triggering injection at a later stage.
questions.option_b: An attack that requires two database servers.
questions.option_c: A UNION query with exactly two columns.
questions.option_d: An SQL error that appears twice.
questions.explanation: The payload may be accepted and stored safely at first, then become dangerous when later incorporated into dynamic SQL.

questions.question: Which mitigation is the primary structural defence against SQL injection?
questions.option_a: Prepared statements / parameterised queries.
questions.explanation: Parameterisation keeps user-supplied values separate from SQL syntax.

questions.question: Why is escaping special characters alone generally weaker than parameterised queries?
questions.option_a: Escaping can be context- and encoding-dependent, while parameterisation separates data from query structure.
questions.option_c: Prepared statements require users to be administrators.
questions.explanation: The lecture emphasises structural separation rather than relying on character blocklists or ad hoc escaping.

questions.question: What is the role of least privilege for a database account?
questions.option_a: Limit damage if the application is compromised through SQL injection.
questions.option_c: Make every user a database administrator.
questions.explanation: A minimally privileged database account limits the actions and data available to an attacker.

questions.question: A WAF blocks the string SELECT but an attacker uses an alternative encoding or syntax. What does this illustrate?
questions.option_a: A WAF blocklist is not a substitute for fixing unsafe query construction.
questions.option_b: SQL injection is impossible through encoded input.
questions.explanation: Blocklists can often be bypassed and do not correct the underlying data/code mixing flaw.

questions.question: Which statement about SQLi database fingerprinting is most accurate?
questions.option_a: Different database engines may expose different syntax, functions and error behaviour.
questions.option_b: Every database supports exactly the same functions.
questions.option_c: Fingerprinting is only possible with source code.
questions.explanation: Engine-specific syntax and behaviour can help identify the backend, but fingerprinting alone is not proof of data extraction.

questions.question: A search field returns no visible data and no errors. A tester sees a consistent conditional delay when a guessed character matches. What is the most defensible conclusion?
questions.option_a: A time-based blind SQLi inference channel may exist; confirm carefully with repeatable controls.
questions.option_c: The application is vulnerable to XXE.
questions.option_d: A 500 error is required to prove SQLi.
questions.explanation: Conditional timing differences can indicate time-based blind SQLi, but repeatability and controls are important to rule out noise.

questions.question: A value is safely inserted using a parameterised INSERT, but a later report concatenates the stored value into dynamic SQL. What is the correct assessment?
questions.option_a: The initial parameterised insert guarantees the value can never cause SQLi.
questions.option_b: The later unsafe query can still create second-order SQL injection.
questions.option_d: The database automatically escapes all stored data forever.
questions.explanation: Parameterising one query does not make a stored value safe for every later query context.

questions.question: What is sqlmap primarily designed to do?
questions.option_a: Automate detection and exploitation of SQL injection in authorised testing.
questions.explanation: sqlmap automates SQL injection testing and related database enumeration tasks.

questions.question: Which sqlmap option supplies a target URL?
questions.option_a: -u
questions.explanation: The -u option specifies the target URL.

questions.question: What does sqlmap’s -r option commonly specify?
questions.option_a: A file containing a raw HTTP request.
questions.explanation: The -r option lets sqlmap read a captured raw HTTP request, including headers and body.

questions.question: Which sqlmap option is used to enumerate database names?
questions.option_a: --tables
questions.explanation: --dbs enumerates available databases.

questions.question: What is the purpose of --tables in sqlmap?
questions.option_a: List tables in the selected database.
questions.option_c: Extract every file on the server.
questions.explanation: --tables enumerates tables, typically in a database selected with -D.

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes sqlmap --level from --risk?
questions.option_a: Level affects the breadth of tests and payloads; risk affects potentially dangerous tests.
questions.option_b: Level sets database privileges; risk sets the URL.
questions.explanation: The lecture treats level as test coverage and risk as the potential impact/danger of tests.

questions.question: Why should a tester understand and manually validate SQL injection before relying on sqlmap?
questions.option_a: Automation can produce false positives or miss context; manual understanding helps interpret and verify results.
questions.option_d: sqlmap only works on local files.
questions.explanation: The lecture’s message is to understand the vulnerability first and use automation as an aid, not a replacement for reasoning.

questions.question: A sqlmap run is producing disruptive requests against a shared production service. What is the appropriate response?
questions.option_a: Increase --risk and continue.
questions.option_b: Stop and ensure explicit authorisation, scope, rate limits and Rules of Engagement before resuming.
questions.option_d: Ignore service impact because automated tools are safe.
questions.explanation: Automated exploitation can affect availability and data. Testing must remain within authorised scope and agreed limits.

questions.question: What is OS command injection?
questions.option_a: Untrusted input is incorporated into an operating-system command and interpreted by a shell.
questions.option_b: A browser sends a SQL query.
questions.option_c: An XML parser resolves an entity.
questions.option_d: A user changes an object ID.
questions.explanation: Command injection occurs when input becomes part of a command interpreted by the operating system or shell.

questions.question: A network diagnostic page accepts a host value. Which input feature may allow command chaining in a vulnerable shell context?
questions.option_a: Shell metacharacters such as ; or &&.
questions.explanation: Shell metacharacters can separate or conditionally chain commands when input is passed unsafely to a shell.

questions.question: What is the key difference between SQL injection and OS command injection?
questions.option_a: They target different interpreters: a database SQL parser versus an operating-system shell/command interpreter.
questions.option_b: SQLi targets browsers and command injection targets CSS.
questions.option_d: Command injection only changes HTTP status codes.
questions.explanation: Both involve data becoming instructions, but the interpreter and resulting impact differ.

questions.question: A command-injection payload produces no visible output. Which approach may help confirm blind execution in an authorised lab?
questions.option_a: A controlled time delay or out-of-band interaction.
questions.option_d: Using an unrelated SQL UNION payload.
questions.explanation: Blind command injection can be inferred through timing or a controlled external callback when direct output is absent.

questions.question: Which tool is specifically mentioned in the lecture for automating OS command injection testing?
questions.option_a: commix
questions.explanation: The lecture identifies commix as a command-injection testing tool.

questions.question: Why is passing an argument array safer than constructing a shell command string?
questions.option_a: It keeps arguments separate and avoids shell interpretation of metacharacters.
questions.option_d: It makes every argument an administrator command.
questions.explanation: Argument arrays avoid unnecessary shell parsing and reduce the chance that input becomes executable shell syntax.

questions.question: A developer removes semicolons from a user-supplied hostname but still concatenates it into a shell command. What is the best assessment?
questions.option_a: The application is secure because one metacharacter is blocked.
questions.option_b: A character blocklist is fragile; use safe APIs/argument arrays and validate the input.
questions.option_d: The server must reject all DNS names.
questions.explanation: Many shell constructs and encodings exist; structural separation is the robust mitigation.

questions.question: A tester sees a DNS callback after submitting input to a diagnostic endpoint, but no output appears in the response. What does this evidence most strongly support?
questions.option_a: A possible out-of-band blind command injection or other server-side callback; isolate the sink and confirm with controls.
questions.explanation: An external interaction can indicate server-side execution or fetching, but the exact vulnerability requires controlled attribution.

questions.question: What does XXE stand for?
questions.option_a: XML External Entity
questions.explanation: XXE is XML External Entity injection.

questions.question: Which XML feature is central to a typical XXE attack?
questions.option_a: DOCTYPE declarations and external entity references.
questions.explanation: XXE abuses XML parser handling of external entities declared through document type definitions.

questions.question: What can a vulnerable XML parser disclose through a file-based XXE payload?
questions.option_a: Files readable by the application process, subject to parser and system restrictions.
questions.option_b: Any file on the internet regardless of access.
questions.explanation: External entities may cause the parser to read local resources accessible to the process.

questions.question: Why can XXE sometimes lead to SSRF?
questions.option_a: An external entity can cause the XML parser/server to request an attacker-selected external or internal resource.
questions.option_b: XXE automatically changes the user’s role.
questions.option_d: SSRF is a type of CSS injection.
questions.explanation: The parser’s external-resource resolution can make server-side requests, overlapping with SSRF behaviour.

questions.question: Which input formats or document types may contain XML that a server processes, as mentioned in the lecture?
questions.option_a: SAML, SVG, DOCX and XLSX.
questions.option_b: JPEG, MP3 and plain PNG only.
questions.explanation: The lecture notes XML can be encountered in APIs, SAML, SVG and Office Open XML document formats.

questions.question: A vulnerable parser does not return file contents in its HTTP response. What technique may still reveal an XXE issue?
questions.option_a: Blind XXE using an external DTD or out-of-band interaction.
questions.option_c: Using Intruder Battering Ram on a password field.
questions.explanation: Blind XXE can use external interactions to signal parser behaviour or exfiltrate data out of band.

questions.question: Which mitigation most directly removes the common XXE attack mechanism?
questions.option_a: Disable DTD processing and external entity resolution in the XML parser.
questions.option_b: Block the word SYSTEM in the browser.
questions.option_d: Move the XML file into the web root.
questions.explanation: Disabling DTDs/external entities prevents the parser from resolving attacker-controlled external resources.

questions.question: What is Server-Side Request Forgery?
questions.option_a: An attacker causes the server to make an HTTP request to a destination selected or influenced by the attacker.
questions.option_b: An attacker makes the browser send a request to itself.
questions.option_c: A database accepts an invalid SQL query.
questions.option_d: A user reads another user’s invoice.
questions.explanation: SSRF abuses server-side URL-fetching functionality to reach destinations from the server’s network position.

questions.question: Which feature is a plausible SSRF entry point?
questions.option_a: A link-preview or import-from-URL feature.
questions.option_b: A local password strength meter that never sends data.
questions.explanation: Features that fetch user-supplied URLs can become SSRF sinks.

questions.question: Why is localhost an interesting SSRF target?
questions.option_a: The server may expose internal services on loopback that external users cannot reach directly.
questions.option_d: It is always the public internet gateway.
questions.explanation: A server-side fetch to localhost can access services from the server’s own network context.

questions.question: Which IPv4 address is the AWS instance metadata endpoint highlighted in the lecture?
questions.explanation: The lecture identifies 169.254.169.254 as the AWS metadata endpoint.

questions.question: What is the key protection added by AWS IMDSv2 compared with IMDSv1?
questions.option_a: A token is required before metadata requests are made.
questions.option_b: Metadata is moved to a public DNS name.
questions.explanation: IMDSv2 requires a session token obtained through a PUT request and supplied in subsequent metadata requests.

questions.question: Which header is shown in the lecture for GCP metadata access?
questions.option_a: X-aws-ec2-metadata-token
questions.explanation: The lecture shows the required GCP metadata header as Metadata-Flavor: Google.

questions.question: A naive SSRF filter blocks the literal string 127.0.0.1. Which technique could bypass such a string-only filter?
questions.option_a: An alternate IP representation such as decimal 2130706433.
questions.explanation: Alternate representations of the same IP can evade simple string blocklists.

questions.question: A URL passes a hostname check because it resolves to a public IP, but resolves to an internal IP when fetched later. What is this technique?
questions.option_a: DNS rebinding
questions.explanation: DNS rebinding exploits a time-of-check/time-of-use gap between validation and the actual request.

questions.question: Which SSRF defence is strongest according to the lecture’s structural approach?
questions.option_a: Block the text localhost and 169.254 only.
questions.option_b: Allowlist exact permitted destinations, validate resolved/final IPs after redirects, block private/link-local ranges and enforce IMDSv2.
questions.option_d: Return raw fetched responses to users.
questions.explanation: A positive destination allowlist plus post-resolution/redirect validation and metadata protections addresses common bypasses.

questions.question: What does ../ typically do in a filesystem path?
questions.option_a: Move one directory upward.
questions.explanation: The parent-directory sequence moves traversal one directory upward.

questions.question: A parameter ?file=report.pdf is concatenated directly into a filesystem path. What is the principal risk?
questions.option_a: The input may escape the intended directory and access other files.
questions.explanation: Unchecked path construction can allow directory traversal and arbitrary file reads within process permissions.

questions.question: Which payload illustrates URL-encoded traversal?
questions.option_a: ..%2f..%2fetc%2fpasswd
questions.explanation: %2f encodes a slash, so the sequence represents encoded ../ traversal components.

questions.question: Why can a single-pass filter that removes ../ be bypassed by a nested sequence such as ....//?
questions.option_a: After one stripping pass, the remaining characters can form ../.
questions.option_b: The payload is a valid JWT.
questions.option_d: The browser converts it to SQL.
questions.explanation: A naive single-pass replacement can leave a traversal sequence behind after removing the middle characters.

questions.question: Which mitigation best prevents path traversal when serving a file from a permitted base directory?
questions.option_a: Canonicalise/resolve the final path and verify it remains inside the allowed base directory; preferably allowlist filenames.
questions.option_b: Remove only the first occurrence of ../.
questions.explanation: Canonicalisation followed by a containment check prevents alternate encodings from escaping the intended directory.

questions.question: What is the dangerous combination that makes an uploaded file capable of becoming a web shell?
questions.option_a: The file is executable by the server and stored somewhere the attacker can reach.
questions.option_b: The file has a long name and a small size.
questions.option_c: The file is uploaded over HTTPS.
questions.option_d: The file has a valid image extension only.
questions.explanation: The lecture identifies server execution plus attacker reachability as the critical combination.

questions.question: Why is the Content-Type header not reliable proof that an uploaded file is an image?
questions.option_a: The client can set or spoof the header.
questions.option_c: It is encrypted by the browser.
questions.option_d: It contains the file’s cryptographic signature.
questions.explanation: Content-Type is supplied as part of the request and can be controlled by an attacker.

questions.question: What is a double-extension upload bypass example from the lecture?
questions.option_a: shell.php.jpg
questions.explanation: A weak extension filter may accept a filename such as shell.php.jpg while server handling may still execute it depending on configuration.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a polyglot upload such as a file beginning with GIF89a followed by PHP code?
questions.option_a: To satisfy a superficial image magic-byte check while retaining executable content.
questions.option_c: To prevent the server from storing the file.
questions.explanation: A polyglot can begin with valid image bytes and also contain content interpreted as code if stored and served unsafely.

questions.question: Which mitigation most strongly prevents a stored upload from executing as a server-side script?
questions.option_a: Store files outside the web root and serve them through a non-executing handler with no-execute permissions.
questions.option_d: Allow uploads to the application source directory.
questions.explanation: Outside-webroot storage and non-executable serving remove the execution path even if validation checks fail.

questions.question: Which pairing correctly matches the vulnerable interpreter or sink?
questions.option_a: SQL injection—database SQL parser; command injection—OS shell.
questions.option_b: SQL injection—XML parser; command injection—browser CSS.
questions.option_d: SQL injection—DNS resolver; command injection—TLS certificate.
questions.explanation: SQLi targets SQL interpretation, while OS command injection targets shell/command interpretation.

questions.question: Which mapping best captures the lecture’s common injection theme?
questions.option_a: SQLi and command injection turn data into instructions; XXE and SSRF can turn input into destinations; traversal and upload can turn input into paths or executable content.
questions.option_b: All six attacks are caused only by weak passwords.
questions.option_c: All six attacks require browser JavaScript.
questions.option_d: All six are prevented by hiding URLs.
questions.explanation: The lecture’s through-line is failure to separate untrusted data from code, destinations, paths or executable files.

questions.question: A developer proposes blocking quotes, semicolons, angle brackets and ../ across all input fields. What is the strongest response?
questions.option_a: This is a complete universal fix.
questions.option_b: Blocklists are fragile and can break legitimate input; use structural controls appropriate to each sink.
questions.explanation: The lecture contrasts blocklists with parameterised queries, argument arrays, disabled XML entities and destination/path allowlists.

questions.question: Which mitigation set is correctly matched to the vulnerability family?
questions.option_a: SQLi—parameterised queries; command injection—argument arrays; XXE—disable external entities; SSRF—destination allowlist.
questions.option_b: SQLi—HttpOnly; command injection—SameSite; XXE—UUIDs; SSRF—password spraying.
questions.option_c: SQLi—file extension allowlist; command injection—CORS; XXE—MFA; SSRF—SQL comments.
questions.option_d: SQLi—robots.txt; command injection—CSS; XXE—TLS; SSRF—JWT encoding.
questions.explanation: Each control structurally prevents untrusted input from becoming executable syntax or an unapproved destination.

questions.question: A URL-import endpoint fetches an internal metadata address, then the application returns the fetched response to the user. Which risk chain is most concerning?
questions.option_a: SSRF may expose cloud metadata and temporary instance-role credentials.
questions.option_c: The request must be SQL injection.
questions.option_d: The only risk is an HTTP 302 redirect.
questions.explanation: The lecture describes SSRF to metadata as a chain that can expose cloud credentials and potentially compromise the cloud account.

questions.question: A web application uses raw input in a SQL query, a shell command and a filesystem path. Which design principle addresses the shared root cause across all three?
questions.option_a: Keep data separate from instructions and destinations using parameterised APIs, argument arrays and canonicalised/allowlisted paths.
questions.option_b: Use one global blacklist of suspicious characters.
questions.option_c: Rely on the browser to validate all fields.
questions.explanation: The common failure is allowing untrusted input to cross into a code or path interpretation context; structural separation is the shared remedy.
